text:
The latch stuck, the way it always had. Marcy pressed her thumb against the left side and it gave. Nate watched her do it.

"Lucky guess," he said.

"Sure."

Inside, everything lay in the outline of its own habit: the tray, a coffee can of mismatched screws, a level with its bubble gone yellow. Nate lifted the claw hammer, weighed it, and set it down in a different spot. Marcy moved it back.

"You want the hammer?"

"I have a hammer."

"I know you have a hammer."

He picked up a tape measure. Scratched into the case, in handwriting too careful to be their father's, were the letters *N.R.* He turned it so they faced his palm.

"That one's yours," she said.

"It's a tape measure."

"I'm just saying whose it is."

"Then I'll take it."

"I didn't say you had to."

A drawer slid open somewhere in the garage and neither of them looked. Marcy found the ratchet, its grip worn smooth where his hand had been. She held it without looking up.

"He kept asking if I'd come look at the truck," Nate said.

"It runs."

"Okay."

"I'm saying it runs. Somebody had to start it every Sunday."

Nate nodded slowly, like a man agreeing to a price. He closed the lid on the tray, then opened it again. The tape measure went into his jacket pocket. Marcy became very interested in the screws.

When he reached to shut the box, she said, "Left side."

He pressed. It held.
